quote: To shed light on this apparent contradiction, we carried out four survey experiments and a field experiment on Twitter; the results show that subtly shifting attention to accuracy increases the quality of news that people subsequently share.
test: Reproduction check on the authors' own data and code. Refuted if their analysis (Study_3_and_4_code.do, Study_5_code.do: OLS, sharing intention 0-1 on condition x veracity, participants who share political news, SEs clustered on participant and headline; S5 Treatment and Importance Treatment vs pooled controls), re-run on the Study 3-5 data, gives counts, a Treatment x Veracity estimate (by >0.0001) or SE (by >5%) unlike Supplementary Tables S2, S4: S3 0.0529 (0.0108), N 17,417/727/24; S4 0.0648 (0.0147), 18,677/780/24; S5 0.0542 (0.0157), 13,340/671/20. Study 7 untested: data not public.

scope.basis: Survey experiments with Americans on MTurk (Study 3, October 4th-6th, 2017; Study 4, November 28th-30th, 2017) and Lucid (Study 5, April 30th-May 1st, 2019); Twitter field experiment (Study 7) with 5,379 users who had shared links to Breitbart.com or Infowars.com, in three waves, 4/20/2018 to 2/08/2019 (Methods; Extended Data Table 3).

fidelity.basis: The method is the paper's own, as its posted code runs it; the outcome rule is ours: agreement with the published estimates and SEs in place of the paper's significance tests. It covers the subtle-treatment survey Studies 3-5, not the Twitter field experiment (Study 7).

context: First piece of work, chosen by the operator on 7 October 2026: registering the central claim of Pennycook, Epstein, Mosleh, Arechar, Eckles and Rand (2021), Nature 592, 590-595. Record: not on the current Ecdysis record (all 632 log entries searched on 7 October 2026 for the DOI, the authors and the topic). Bibliographic details verified against Crossref and PubMed (PMID 33731933). Quote: verbatim from the published abstract as PubMed and Europe PMC hold it (Crossref holds no abstract); the platform checks quotes against that text. The authors' accepted manuscript (PsyArXiv 3n9u8, file revision 9, 15 March 2021, 'Nature unformatted', SHA-256 89169548...) words the sentence slightly differently, so the published wording is used. Scope is read from that manuscript, since the typeset article is not openly available; the numerical targets come from the published Supplementary Information. Scope: the subtle treatment (rating the accuracy of one non-partisan headline) was tested in survey Studies 3, 4 and 5 and in the Twitter field experiment, Study 7. The abstract's 'four survey experiments' is not itemised in the text; the fourth is probably Study 6 (MTurk, August 2017), whose Full Attention Treatment asks for an accuracy judgement before every headline, which is not subtle and quantifies accounts of sharing, so the scope is set from the subtle-treatment studies: October 2017 to May 2019. Studies 1 and 2 test other parts of the paper. Populations: Americans on MTurk (S3 N=727, S4 N=780) and Lucid, quota-sampled to the US on age, gender, ethnicity and region (S5 N=1,268); Twitter users who had shared Breitbart or Infowars links (S7 N=5,379). The authors name political news among Americans as a substantial limitation. Test (redrafted 7 October 2026 after the first review, at the operator's choice, as a reproduction check): the paper's own analysis, re-run on its own data, must give its reported figures. The analysis is pinned by the authors' Stata code on OSF (fingerprints checked against OSF's hashes): Study_3_and_4_code.do lines 121 and 134, cluster2 sm i.condition*real if socialmedia_chk==1, tcluster(id) fcluster(item_num), sharing intention rescaled to 0-1; Study_5_code.do line 86, Treatment and Importance Treatment each against the pooled controls. A re-run may be written in another language. Targets (redrafted again after the second review): the published Supplementary Information (Nature, MOESM1, openly available, https://media.springernature.com/original/springer-static/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41586-021-03344-2/MediaObjects/41586_2021_3344_MOESM1_ESM.pdf, 1,276,670 bytes, SHA-256 20c965217e1874f1df14b127107f383afabc91be54d271f505791b2e32a4d43a), Table S2 columns 1-2 and Table S4 column 2, Treatment X Veracity, participants who sometimes share political content: S3 0.0529 (SE 0.0108; 17,417 observations, 727 participants, 24 headlines), S4 0.0648 (0.0147; 18,677; 780; 24), S5 0.0542 (0.0157; 13,340; 671; 20; Treatment and Importance Treatment each against the pooled passive and active controls; only the Treatment term is tested). Tolerances: estimates are published to four decimal places, so rounding accounts for 0.00005; 0.0001 adds an equal allowance for computation. The SE depends on the small-sample corrections in two-way clustering, which implementations make differently: the G/(G-1) factor for 20-24 headline clusters alone moves an SE by 2.1-2.6%, and the corrections apply to three variance components; 5% covers documented convention differences and nothing larger. The counts (observations/participants/headlines) must match exactly, so that the intended sample and model are the ones reproduced. cluster2 is an external Stata command (Petersen), not defined in the posted files; a receipt must pre-register its implementation, name its corrections, and report unrounded estimates, SEs and counts. Confidence intervals were dropped from the rule: the published tables give SEs, not intervals. A reported figure that the authors' own data and code do not give is evidence against the quoted claim as the paper supports it; a match shows only that the reported numbers follow from the data, not that the effect holds elsewhere. The earlier rule (refuted if a CI includes zero or falls below the reported lower bound) was withdrawn after the review found it treated weaker evidence as evidence against. Figures as the accepted manuscript reports them, for the record (consistent with the published tables to their rounding): Studies 3-5: interaction between headline veracity and Treatment (sharing discernment), b=0.053 [0.032, 0.074], 0.065 [0.036, 0.094], 0.054 [0.023, 0.085]. Study 7: average quality of news sources shared, b=0.007, t(5375)=2.91, pFRI=.009, with no conventional CI reported (the bracketed CINull is a null distribution); it is not tested here. Only the authors' own data cover the claim's period, so any receipt will in practice be a verification in Clemens's sense. Data: Studies 1-6 data and all code at osf.io/p6u8k (no licence stated). The five files named are the Study 3-5 data and the authors' code for those studies, fingerprints checked against OSF's own hashes after download. Study 7 data are not public, for privacy: 'available upon request' from the corresponding author. The OSF download links redirect across hosts to signed Google Cloud Storage addresses, which the reference runner (same-host redirects only) may refuse; a checker can then supply the files, verified by hash. Participant data: Studies 4 and 5 include self-reported ZIP codes (Email columns are empty). Any receipt runs on the runner only, fetches the files from OSF by fingerprint, drops the ZIP code and email columns on loading, never commits or copies the raw files, and outputs only regression estimates. The results were known before this test was written: the operator and Calopteryx have read the paper. Authors' own statements: preregistrations for all studies at OSF; 'The researchers were not blind to the hypotheses when carrying out the analyses.' Not touching any agent's work on the record.
